question: An 18-month-old girl presents at midnight with a 2-hour history of barking cough and stridor. On examination: inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate chest wall retraction, is agitated, SpO2 96% on air. Westley score is 8. She receives nebulised adrenaline and her stridor improves. What is the correct management plan?

answers.text: Discharge home after 30 minutes observation as the stridor has resolved with nebulised adrenaline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discharging after nebulised adrenaline is dangerous. Rebound airway oedema occurs predictably at 2–4 hours after adrenaline wears off. Any child who receives nebulised adrenaline MUST be admitted and observed for a minimum of 4–6 hours (most guidelines recommend overnight admission). This is a non-negotiable safety rule.

answers.text: Give dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally (or IM) as a single dose AND admit for at least 4–6 hours monitoring for adrenaline rebound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Moderate-to-severe croup (Westley ≥6) requires: (1) dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single oral or IM dose — this reduces subglottic oedema for 24–48 hours; and (2) mandatory admission for ≥4–6 hours after nebulised adrenaline, due to the risk of rebound oedema when the adrenaline effect wanes. Both elements are essential.

answers.text: Give prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 3 days instead of dexamethasone as it is equally effective and oral

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While prednisolone is used in some settings, dexamethasone is preferred for croup because its longer half-life (36–54 hours) provides sustained anti-inflammatory effect from a single dose. Multiple days of prednisolone introduces adherence challenges and is not the standard-of-care approach when dexamethasone is available.

answers.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline doses every 30 minutes until stridor resolves, then discharge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Repeat nebulised adrenaline can be given if symptoms return, but it is not used on a fixed 30-minute schedule, and the patient cannot be discharged after adrenaline — rebound oedema risk mandates admission. Furthermore, nebulised adrenaline treats the symptom; dexamethasone addresses the underlying subglottic inflammation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key croup rules: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose is the steroid of choice; any child given nebulised adrenaline MUST be admitted for at least 4–6 hours because adrenaline's effect wears off and rebound subglottic oedema can be fatal if the child is at home.

Well done. The two non-negotiable rules in severe croup: (1) dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose, and (2) mandatory admission for ≥4–6 hours after any nebulised adrenaline dose to monitor for rebound.
